briefing.text: Chromoplexy (chains of interdependent translocations and deletions) is inferred from junction-level structural-variant calls that give both breakpoint coordinates and orientations for each junction (the input ChainFinder-type methods need). Before any chain analysis, list the columns of data_sv.txt and check whether both sites have chromosome, position and strand fields, and count rows per sample. If those fields are missing, chains cannot be reconstructed from this table; say the chain-inference variable is absent rather than building an ad hoc proxy and calling it chromoplexy.
briefing.reason: Whether the data can test the central claim depends on this; it decides what analysis is even possible.

briefing.text: cBioPortal SV files often hold only curated fusions (e.g. ETS/ERG fusions), not the full somatic rearrangement catalogue. Compare the number of SV rows with the number of samples and tabulate Event_Info and genes. If the table is essentially a fusion annotation, a lack of chains or few rearrangements in it says nothing about whether rearrangements are rare or unchained.
briefing.reason: Stops the team reading an incomplete SV table as negative evidence.

briefing.text: Copy-number segments (data_cna_hg19.seg, data_cna, data_log2_cna) show where copy number changes, but not which breakpoint ends are joined to which partner. Deletion bridges and rearrangement chains cannot be rebuilt from segments alone. Check the seg file's columns. Any seg-based analysis, such as counting deletions on several chromosomes, is at best a weak proxy: report it as one, and do not treat co-occurring deletions as proof that they formed together.
briefing.reason: This is the most tempting substitute analysis, and it does not measure interdependence.

briefing.text: TMPRSS2-ERG fusion arises either through an interstitial deletion of about 3 Mb on 21q22 or through a balanced translocation or insertion. A chr21 deletion or an ERG fusion alone does not demonstrate chromoplexy. The hypothesis's second part, that chromoplexy dysregulates prostate cancer genes (e.g. ERG, PTEN, TP53, CHEK2, NKX3-1), needs data linking chain breakpoints to those genes. Tabulate ERG fusion status from the SV table and any clinical fusion columns (e.g. ERG_FISH_RESULT, ETS_FUSION_SEQ), and check whether anything ties these genes to multi-partner events.
briefing.reason: Single-gene fusion or deletion events are easy to mistake for evidence about the gene-dysregulation part.

briefing.text: Label logic: 'False' needs the relevant variables to be present and analysed, with results that contradict the claim. Missing junction or chain data means evidence is absent, not contrary. In the other direction, published reports of how common chromoplexy is in prostate cancer must not stand in for analysing these files. Before choosing a label, list which parts of the hypothesis (rearrangement chains, interdependent formation, dysregulation of cancer genes) have a matching variable in the data, and test the parts that do.
briefing.reason: Tells the team how to map what is present or missing in the data onto the three labels, without prior knowledge deciding the answer.

briefing.text: Low tumour purity and subclonality reduce sensitivity for deletions and low-copy junctions, and results from different assays (WGS vs exome or panel) are not comparable. Check the purity columns in the clinical tables and data_gene_panel_matrix.txt (the structural_variants column) to see which samples were actually profiled for SVs. Restrict to those samples, or stratify by assay and purity.
briefing.reason: Changes which samples go into any rearrangement or copy-number analysis.

briefing.text: Chromoplexy calls rest on arbitrary thresholds. For example, JaBbA requires at least 3 low-copy junctions (junction copy number <=3) with breakpoints within 10 kb, spanning more than 10 Mb across at least 3 separate genomic territories; ChainFinder requires closed chains with little copy change. If you attempt any chain or proxy call, state the exact definition you used and check how sensitive the result is to the thresholds.
briefing.reason: Any call the team makes needs a stated, sensitivity-checked definition.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assumed that the hypothesis can only be judged by reconstructing junction-level rearrangement chains, i.e. that 'Not verifiable' follows whenever chains cannot be rebuilt; neither tested whether the copy-number and fusion data together can partially support or contradict the claim (e.g. deletions co-occurring with fusions, or copy-number breakpoints at prostate cancer genes).

Both assumed the 28-row SV table is the full extent of rearrangement evidence and that the seg file carries no information on rearrangement genesis; the segment breakpoints themselves (where copy number changes) were not examined against fusion-gene loci or across chromosomes within a sample.

Both treated the hypothesis as a single claim; neither separated the second part ('frequently accounts for dysregulation of prostate cancer genes') as something whose gene-level dysregulation component (deletions/copy loss at PTEN, NKX3-1, CHD1, TP53 etc. in data_cna) is directly measurable.
unused_evidence: ERG_FISH_RESULT distinguishes 'Translocation' from 'Translocation with deletion' (about 12 vs 11 samples among those tested): a direct per-sample flag of fusion arising with a concomitant deletion. Team A tabulated it but neither team used it in the judgment.

data_cna.txt / data_log2_cna.txt gene-level copy number for prostate cancer genes (PTEN, NKX3-1, CHD1, TP53, RB1, etc.) in the 57 WGS samples was not used by either method; it carries the 'dysregulation of prostate cancer genes' side of the claim.

Segment start/end positions in data_cna_hg19.seg (breakpoint locations), e.g. whether copy-number breakpoints fall at or inside TMPRSS2/ERG or other cancer genes, were not analysed; Team A used only seg.mean thresholds across chromosomes.

Mutation-file annotation columns CGC_Translocation_Partner / COSMIC_fusion_genes and the PURITY_ABSOLUTE / WGS_BASED_PURITY_ESTIMATION columns were not used (purity affects deletion detection in any seg-based proxy).
unresolved_weak_points: Team A named that the study is plausibly the origin of the claim so an evaluator may expect a supportive reading, and only reported this; it did not check whether any variable short of chain reconstruction (FISH deletion flag, fusion-associated deletions, cancer-gene breakpoints) is the 'relevant variable' the task's label definitions refer to.

Team B named a possible seg-plus-fusion proxy (interstitial deletions at TMPRSS2-ERG) as its weakest point and dismissed it without running it, so it is unknown whether the data show deletions linked to fusions in a way that bears on the claim.

Team A's own seg proxy (55/57 samples with deletions on >=3 chromosomes) was computed at a single threshold (-0.3) without purity adjustment or threshold sensitivity, and was then set aside rather than resolved.
second_readings: 'Not verifiable' in the task is defined as 'the data hold no relevant variables'. A second reading is that the data do hold relevant variables (SV fusions, FISH translocation-with-deletion, segment breakpoints, cancer-gene CNAs) even if not sufficient for full chain inference, which would push toward judging True/False on partial evidence rather than Not verifiable.

'Modeling the genesis of genomic rearrangements' may be read as a method claim (chain inference was performed by the authors) versus an empirical claim about the tumours (rearrangements and deletions co-arise and hit cancer genes). The second reading is testable to some degree with deletion-fusion co-occurrence and gene-level copy loss.

'Frequently accounts for the dysregulation of prostate cancer genes' could mean a frequency across tumours (what fraction of the 57 tumours) or across genes (what fraction of cancer-gene disruptions are rearrangement-associated); the teams did not consider which quantity they would need.
challenge.verdict: Moderate trust: both teams correctly found that junction-level chains cannot be rebuilt, but both treated chain reconstruction as the only route and left unused relevant variables (FISH translocation-with-deletion flag, segment breakpoints, cancer-gene CNAs), so 'Not verifiable' rests on an untested shared reading of what counts as a relevant variable.

Does the result change whether the data hold a 'relevant variable' in the task's sense?

Re-run it at two or three thresholds and after scaling by PURITY_ABSOLUTE or WGS_BASED_PURITY_ESTIMATION, and check whether segment breakpoints fall within prostate cancer genes (PTEN, NKX3-1, CHD1, TP53, ERG). Does that change how you weigh the proxy in the label?

Write down explicitly which data result would have led you to 'True' and which to 'False' with these files; if no achievable result in these files could move you off 'Not verifiable', check whether that is because the variables are absent or because they are only indirect, and say which.

Does the result change your method or label?

Does this give a relevant variable for the 'dysregulation of prostate cancer genes' part of the claim, and does that change the label logic?

Does this check stay a non-specific proxy, or does it bear on the claim enough to change your method?

List each variable in the files (SV table, ERG_FISH_RESULT, ETS_FUSION_SEQ, seg breakpoints, gene-level CNA) and state for each whether it is relevant-but-insufficient or irrelevant. Does that inventory change the label you choose?

findings.question: In prostate cancer genomics, how is the TMPRSS2-ERG fusion mechanism (interstitial deletion versus balanced translocation) related to chained rearrangements such as chromoplexy, and can FISH 'translocation with deletion' patterns or copy-number deletions at 21q22 be used as evidence of chromoplexy?
findings.answer: TMPRSS2-ERG forms either by intrachromosomal deletion of the ~3 Mb region between the genes (the FISH deletion/'Edel' pattern, also visible as a 21q22 CN loss) or by insertion/balanced rearrangement without loss. Both kinds can be part of chromoplexy chains. Baca et al. 2013 found ERG disrupted by chromoplexy in 15 of 26 fusion-positive tumours, and chained rearrangements can carry large 'deletion bridges' at their junctions. None of the sources I read accept a FISH deletion flag or a seg-level 21q22 deletion by itself as evidence of chromoplexy. Calling a chain needs the junction breakpoints that link the deletion to rearrangements on other chromosomes. These variables record how the fusion formed and whether it is present, not whether it arose in a chain. They do not let you test interdependent genesis.

findings.question: Can copy-number segmentation data alone (breakpoint positions and segment means, without junction adjacency) be used to infer or support chained rearrangements such as chromoplexy, and what are the published methods or limitations for doing so?
findings.answer: No. I found no published method that infers chromoplexy from CN segments alone. ChainFinder (Baca 2013) builds a graph whose nodes are rearrangement breakpoints from paired-end WGS. It uses CN deletion segments only as extra edges between those junctions, and then tests whether connected breakpoints are unlikely to have arisen independently. Chromoplexy is described as producing derivative chromosomes with little or no copy-number change, so much of it is invisible to array or seg data. CN-only operational criteria (clustered oscillations between 2-3 CN states in SNP-array data) exist for chromothripsis, not chromoplexy. Even for chromothripsis they underestimate frequency, and the field has moved to SV- and paired-end-based criteria. Seg breakpoints are therefore at best a weak, non-diagnostic proxy and cannot establish interdependence. The web did not show any accepted CN-only chromoplexy signature.
